news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders forecasts £1.78m education overspend for 2026/27 after £1.735m budget transfers
news_drafts.lead:
Education and Children's Services at Scottish Borders Council is forecasting a net overspend of £1.78m for 2026/27, according to the September revenue monitoring report before the Executive Committee on 10 November. The figure is after temporary transfers of budget from two other services: £0.79m from Finance and £0.86m from Infrastructure and Environment.

Before the transfers, the service's projected outturn variance for the year is £3.517m. The appendix to the report gives the proposed transfer as £1.735m, which leaves the net overspend at £1.781m. The papers attribute the pressure mainly to external placements and Home to School Transport. Underspends in Additional Support Needs partly offset them.

The report also says workforce pressures are adding to costs. It cites absence and maternity cover in schools.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders used its own cash instead of £111.3m of borrowing at March 2026, down from £127.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Scottish Borders Council ended 2025/26 having used its own spare cash, rather than taking out loans, to pay for £111.3m of spending on long-lasting assets such as buildings and roads. A year earlier the figure was £127.9m. The figures are in the council's annual treasury management report (how it borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both), which went to its Audit Committee on 21 September 2026.

The papers measure this against the capital financing requirement, the total the council has spent on long-lived assets that it has not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow. Using cash in place of a loan is known as internal borrowing, which saves interest but uses up the council's own cushion. The report says the council "has again, where possible, deferred borrowing using surplus cash rather than undertaking new borrowing". It describes this as a deliberate policy and puts the fall in the figure down to lower expected capital demands.

An appendix to the report compares the requirement one year ahead with the council's external debt, the total of all loans it owes. On that basis the council "remains under-borrowed by £65.9m at the end of 2025/26", the paper says.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders pension fund cash deficit widens as pensioners outnumber active members
news_drafts.lead: The Scottish Borders Council pension fund faces a structural cash deficit as pensioner numbers have grown to exceed active member numbers for the first time, with one pensioner now for every active member employed. Over the year to June 2026, pension payments and costs of £366m outstripped contributions by £9m, a shortfall the fund must cover from investment returns and reserves. Pensioner membership has risen 28% over five years while active members grew just 2.9%, a demographic shift that began when the fund matured in 2013/14. This year the fund delivered a 5.7% investment return, the lowest among Scotland's 11 local government pension schemes and well below its 12.3% benchmark; the fund has since terminated underperforming equity managers and committed to changes. Despite the cash flows, Audit Scotland's draft annual report concluded the fund has effective governance and financial management arrangements in place. The council's employer contribution rate was cut to 17% from 18.5% following a strong 134% funding valuation in 2023.

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 (a) - Treasury Management Midyear Report 2026-27 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: The PWLB 25-year certainty rate rose from 6.20% on 1 April 2026 to 6.67% on 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the whole gilt and PWLB curve moved higher over the period, on inflation concerns and a pessimistic fiscal outlook. The 10-year rate moved from 5.62% to 6.17% over the same period.
findings.matters: The cost of long-dated PWLB funding is the number a council weighs against replacing LOBO and maturing debt, so a finance director at another council would want to see the change.
findings.figures: 25-year PWLB certainty rate 6.20% (01/04/2026) to 6.67% (30/09/2026); 10-year 5.62% to 6.17%; 25-year average 6.40%
findings.quote: the general trend has been for the whole curve to shift higher on the back of inflation concerns and a pessimistic outlook for fiscal aspects

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 (a) - Treasury Management Midyear Report 2026-27 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: The financing costs ratio is reported at 9.1% (PI-3A, including IFRS 16 leases) and 8.3% (PI-3B, excluding them) in the 2026/27 revised estimate.
findings.detail: The paper says it now presents both bases side by side, at members' request, so the effect of the IFRS 16 adjustment is visible. The paper gives the 2025/26 PI-3B comparator as 7.5%.
findings.matters: A council that presents its financing costs both with and without leases shows how much of its affordability ratio comes from leasing rather than borrowing, which a peer council could copy.
findings.quote: The intention is to allow members to see both the statutory indicator (PI-3A) and an adjusted indicator (PI-3B) that better reflects the impact of traditional treasury borrowing on revenue resources

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 (a) - Treasury Management Midyear Report 2026-27 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: The council achieved a 3.82% weighted average return on investments in the first six months, and year-to-date performance is £78k above budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the return is 9 basis points above the SONIA average benchmark. It expects returns to be higher in the second half, as interest rates rise and Scottish Government revenue grant payments move from weekly to monthly.
findings.matters: Investment income running ahead of budget in a rising rate environment is a useful benchmark for peers managing short-term cash.
findings.figures: 3.82% weighted average return; SONIA benchmark +9bps; £78k above budget; annual investment return budget £1m; average funds available £28.6m
findings.quote: The Council achieved a weighted average rate of return of 3.82% in the first six months of the year

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 (a) - Treasury Management Midyear Report 2026-27 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: An interest-free Salix loan of £0.3m matured in October 2026 and was repaid in full.
findings.detail: The paper says the second £0.3m Salix loan, due August 2027, will also be repaid and not refinanced.
findings.matters: An early repayment with no replacement funding reduces the council's debt, which is a change a peer council would want to track.
findings.figures: £0.3m repaid; second £0.3m due August 2027 to be repaid and not refinanced
findings.quote: came to Maturity in October 2026 and has been repaid in full.

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 (a) - Treasury Management Midyear Report 2026-27 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: £99.6m of external debt falls due within 12 months of 15 October 2026, up from £84.9m at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says new loans have largely been taken on a shorter term basis, because the advisers expect interest rates to fall. Debt due in one to two years stands at £80.0m, up from £51.6m at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: A large short-dated maturity profile means more frequent refinancing, which lenders and peers would want to see when assessing rollover risk.
findings.figures: Under 12 months £99.6m at 15 Oct 2026, £84.9m at 31 March 2026; 1-2 years £80.0m, £51.6m at 31 March 2026; total external debt £377.0m, £399.0m
findings.quote: In line with advice from the Council’s external advisor’s, new loans have largely been taken on a shorter term basis in recognition of the expectation that interest rates will continue to fall.
